name: Jade Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so please tell me what you'd say in public and what you think privately. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Jade, 43, and I started this junior developer job after a two-year college diploma. I fix account forms for a tech company, usually with my supervisor looking over the tricky parts; I like seeing a customer finally reach the confirmation screen. The hard part is being slow at a problem when I know the mortgage date and our two school-age children are waiting at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my colleagues the new bug sorter is fine if it doesn't hide a complaint from a customer. I still open each report and check the screen where the person got stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, little change in AI would not make our mortgage easier. I'm a junior developer at 43 after a two-year diploma, earn less than most developers, and we have less than a month of expenses saved. My partner's school kitchen hours vary, and there are hardly any nearby software jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing the account forms and ask my supervisor to show me the next part of the code before each weekly release. If the quiet year gives us steady hours, we'd put 20 from each payday into a separate mortgage buffer; if the kitchen hours fall, that transfer stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious already. A small bug sorter won't stop a boiler repair or one short kitchen week from emptying our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What bill came close to upsetting the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the boiler made a knocking sound and we paid for a visit from the repairer. Our older child asked whether we could still pay for the school trip, and I said I'd check the numbers after Friday's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask your supervisor rather than use an AI answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to learn the code slowly from my supervisor, not from an answer box that sounds certain when it's wrong. I would rather admit I need another explanation than send a broken form to customers.

say: I'd accept a **bug sorter** if I still check each customer report.
I'd say **account forms** need a person to test where users get stuck.
think: I worry about the **mortgage and boiler** with under a month saved.
My **junior pay** leaves little room when my partner's kitchen hours fall.
do: Keep fixing **account forms** and ask my supervisor for code explanations.
Save **20 each payday** for mortgage costs only if both sets of hours hold.
feel: **Anxious** about ordinary bills even if AI changes little.
S0.quote: A small bug sorter won't stop a boiler repair or one short kitchen week from emptying our account.
fieldNote: **Household bills** already strain a junior wage and variable kitchen hours under AI Plateau.
Her reluctance to use AI comes with a **specific learning habit**: ask a supervisor and test the customer screen.

steps.text: Keep fixing account forms and checking each customer report
Save 20 each payday for mortgage costs if both sets of hours hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say writing and checking code are most of my day, so the company should tell us whether the junior posts will still be there. A faster tool is not a good answer if customers cannot finish a form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could be cut first. I am still learning, and the company could ask one experienced developer to check AI fixes instead of paying two juniors; my partner's kitchen wage cannot cover the mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep testing account forms while asking my supervisor which tests will stay with people and keeping a notebook of faults I can reproduce. If the company starts replacing routine fixes in the first year, I'd plan extra school-kitchen shifts with my partner only if they agree and paid shifts exist, and we'd stop paying for the children's weekend club before missing the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can picture a layoff meeting that sounds ordinary until my name is on the list. I wake up thinking about the mortgage date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which spending would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The club is the first thing we can pause without breaking the mortgage payment. I would tell our children it is a money choice for now, not because they did anything wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the supervisor's limited time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My supervisor has time for one question at the end of the day. I would bring the failed form and the steps I tried, so I am asking for help with a real fault rather than for a promise of job safety.

say: I'd ask whether **junior posts** survive when AI writes routine fixes.
I'd say **customer forms** still need a real-world check.
think: I expect **my junior role** to be vulnerable as routine code shrinks.
I know my partner's **kitchen wage** cannot carry the mortgage alone.
do: Keep **testing account forms** and record reproducible faults while asking what human checks remain.
Plan **extra kitchen shifts** with my partner only if they agree and paid shifts exist.
Pause the **children's weekend club** before any missed mortgage payment.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely cut and the mortgage due date.
S1.quote: I can picture a layoff meeting that sounds ordinary until my name is on the list.
fieldNote: **Junior code and tests** are directly exposed, and she expects her post could be among early cuts.
Her immediate choices are **conditional and household-level**: partner consent, extra shifts and pausing a club before mortgage arrears.

steps.text: Keep testing account forms and record reproducible faults in a notebook
Plan extra school-kitchen shifts only if partner agrees and paid shifts exist
Pause children's weekend club before missing a mortgage payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people full thinking AI by 2028 reaches our form code almost at once; robots around 2031 won't delay a desk job. I would want a clear answer about final pay and who still helps customers when a form fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior job to go, and I cannot pay the mortgage for long from a cushion under one month. At 43, with two children at school and few local developer vacancies, I cannot become a new specialist in two years just by wanting to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd get the mortgage balance and payment dates together and ask the lender what hardship terms exist if my wage stops. If I lost my job in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for paid school office work only if a vacancy exists and the wage plus my partner's hours cover the mortgage; meanwhile I'd ask my sister whether she could help with school pickups, not money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed and tired. Calling the mortgage lender won't give us back a month's lost wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What help could your sister realistically give?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister has helped with pickups before when both of us worked late. I would ask again only if her own schedule permits; I don't want to turn her into free childcare by assumption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children if work stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children we were checking every bill and that school stays the same for now. If a move became necessary, we would talk to them before putting the house up for sale, but I cannot decide that tonight.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** reaches our code before 2031 robots matter.
I'd ask for **final-pay clarity** and a human route for failed forms.
think: I expect to lose **my junior wage** with less than a month saved.
I cannot assume a **new specialist career** in two years with children and few nearby jobs.
do: Ask the **mortgage lender** now about hardship terms if my wage stops.
After a cut, apply for **school office posts** only if vacancies and household wages cover the mortgage.
Ask my **sister for pickups** only if her schedule permits.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely wage loss and little cash time.
S2.quote: Calling the mortgage lender won't give us back a month's lost wage.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches her desk work in 2028; later robots provide no useful delay.
She has a **contingency list**, but every outside job and family pickup depends on availability and mortgage-covering wages.

steps.text: Ask mortgage lender now about hardship terms if wage stops
Apply for vacant school office posts after a cut only if household wages cover mortgage
Ask sister for school pickups after dismissal only if her schedule permits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years until 2031 gives the company time to tell us which human checks it still pays for. Robots around 2034 are later; the thinking AI reaches my forms and tests in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be able to finish learning the whole account system before then, but I can't count on that keeping my junior post. Five years could let us reduce the mortgage balance if our hours stay steady; it does not make our present buffer any thicker by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for one afternoon a month shadowing the experienced developer on difficult account faults, if my supervisor can spare the time. I'd keep the mortgage buffer transfer at 20 a payday when both wages permit, and in the first year after 2031 I'd apply for paid support-desk posts only if those jobs exist and pay enough with my partner's hours to meet the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious rather than frozen. Five years lets me learn in small pieces. A short month of my partner's school-kitchen shifts could still undo our mortgage plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would shadowing actually involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shadowing means watching how a bad account record is traced and then trying the next one under supervision. If work is too busy to release me, I'd keep doing the forms I know and ask again next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not pay for a course we cannot afford. A paid support post would matter more to us than a certificate with no wage attached.

say: I'd ask which **human checks** the firm will still pay for by 2031.
I'd say **2034 robots** arrive later than the thinking AI changing forms.
think: I could learn **more of the system** in five years, but my post may still go.
I need **steady household hours** before a smaller mortgage balance is possible.
do: Shadow **difficult account faults** monthly if my supervisor can spare time.
Save **20 a payday** when both wages permit.
After 2031, apply for **paid support work** only if jobs exist and household pay meets the mortgage.
feel: **Anxious**, with room to learn but no spare cash guarantee.
S3.quote: A short month of my partner's school-kitchen shifts could still undo our mortgage plan.
fieldNote: **Five years** permit supervised learning, not a guarantee that junior software work remains.
Her mortgage-buffer saving and any support-desk move depend on **both wages**, actual vacancies and paid work.

steps.text: Shadow experienced developer on difficult account faults monthly if supervisor releases time
Save 20 each payday only while both wages permit
Apply after 2031 for vacant support posts only if household pay covers mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 gives children time to grow and adults time to make a plan, but thinking AI still reaches code before robots around 2039. Our company ought to be clear about paid work rather than point at a far date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 53 I might be in customer support or doing something else, but I cannot promise that. The mortgage is due now, my junior wage is low now, and our buffer is still under a month; ten years will only help if we keep earning and get room to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning one account feature at a time and maintain the notebook of faults. If both wages hold, we'd put 20 per payday into the mortgage buffer and review the payment every six months; in the first year after 2036 I'd compare paid support and software posts, moving only if a real offer covers the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious about money, though less frightened by the distant AI date. The mortgage cannot wait ten years for a better software job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger child?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our younger child will be finishing school by then, but I wouldn't choose their studies around a guess about robots. I'd tell them to learn what they like and check the cost before signing up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What learning would help next week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want my supervisor to tell me which part of the account system I can take on next week. A skill I use at work is easier to defend than a certificate we borrowed money to buy.

say: I'd say **2036 thinking AI** reaches code before 2039 robots.
I'd ask my firm to name **paid future work** rather than rely on a distant date.
think: I cannot ignore **today's mortgage** or my thin savings just because 2036 is far away.
I might change fields by 53, but I need **steady wages** first.
do: Keep a **fault notebook** and learn account features at work.
Save **20 per payday** if both wages hold, reviewing mortgage payments every six months.
After 2036, move only for a **real offer** whose pay covers the mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about present bills, though the distant date allows smaller steps.
S4.quote: The mortgage cannot wait ten years for a better software job.
fieldNote: **Current mortgage pressure** survives a distant AI date; low pay and a thin buffer keep her anxious.
She favours **workplace learning** and a conditional wage-covering move over a debt-funded course.

steps.text: Maintain account fault notebook and learn one work feature at a time
Save 20 per payday if both wages hold and review mortgage every six months

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I would have almost no time to replace my wage. Clear notice, mortgage help if hours stop, and a real paid vacancy near home would help; a course without wages would not.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why I changed careers so late. The shop where I worked shut, and the college diploma gave me a way into this job; I'm proud I became a developer at 43, even if I still need help with code.

headlineQuote: I'm proud I became a developer at 43, even if I still need help with code.
portrait: Jade, **43**, is a junior software developer after a two-year diploma and a late move from a closed shop.
Her **lower pay**, under-month savings and variable kitchen wages strain a mortgage and two school-age children's costs.
She avoids AI tools and learns account forms through **supervisor help** and a notebook of real faults.
Steady disruption **alarms** her because routine junior code may shrink; 2028 AGI threatens her wage before robots arrive.
More time permits **supervised learning** and tiny conditional savings, but current mortgage pressure keeps her anxious.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her junior wage before she can fund a search or meet the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear notice**, mortgage help if wages stop and a nearby paid vacancy would give her options.
